title: Taylorism: Work Faster!
summary: Josh and Chuck (iHeart Intro speaker, referred to as Chuck) examine Frederick Winslow Taylor and Taylorism, the scientific management movement that broke work into timed, standardized motions and pushed worker output higher. They cover Taylor's Midvale Steel and Bethlehem Steel work, the fictional pig-iron loader Schmidt and the "high priced man" pep talk, the 1911 congressional hearing and Louis Brandeis's railroad rate argument, and the Watertown Arsenal strike that led to a federal ban on Taylor's methods. The episode also covers Frank and Lillian Gilbreth's motion study ("therbligs"), the Gilbreths' family life (the basis of Cheaper by the Dozen), Lillian Gilbreth's home economics and kitchen work triangle, Flora Rose and Martha Van Rensselaer's domestic science, efficiency ideas in schools, deskilling of workers, and computers and algorithmic management as a modern continuation. The episode closes with listener mail from Stanley.

entities.name: On the Art of Cutting Metals

segments.title: Opening banter and forty-five minute timing
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, joking about the timekeeping and introducing the topic of Frederick Taylor and his efficiency system.

segments.title: Efficiency as a 1900s political idea
segments.summary: The hosts set up the Industrial Revolution context of corporations and middle managers, and note that efficiency was a neutral or even progressive goal for reformers who hoped it would bring workers free time and higher wages.

segments.title: Taylor's background and Midvale Steel experiments
segments.summary: Taylor's family and early career are described, including his Harvard-bound eyesight issue, his engineering work at Enterprise Hydraulic Works and Midvale Steel, his thirty thousand metal-cutting experiments, and his 1907 book On the Art of Cutting Metals.
topics: On the Art of Cutting Metals

segments.title: Laziness versus efficiency and systematic soldiering
segments.summary: Chuck shares a film-set anecdote about working smarter, and the hosts discuss Taylor's term systematic soldiering for slacking off and how it relates to Parkinson's law.

segments.title: Time studies and the consulting career
segments.summary: Taylor at Midvale sets up an estimating department to time workers' tasks and sets incentives, then turns himself into a paid consulting engineer. The hosts note this helped create later management consulting firms.

segments.title: Pig iron loading at Bethlehem Steel and the Schmidt story
segments.summary: Taylor's pig-iron experiment at Bethlehem Steel is described: strong workers loaded far beyond the average rate, then a quota was set. The hosts discuss the arbitrary 40 percent rest deduction, the 'law of heavy laboring,' and the fictional worker Schmidt used as a sales anecdote about being a 'high priced man.'

segments.title: Worker pushback and the 1911 congressional hearing
segments.summary: Taylor's remarks at the House committee hearing are discussed, including the 'singing bird' line and William Wilson's rebuttal, and Taylor's attempt to get Wilson's copy of his book. Bethlehem Steel fires Taylor and he asks for a large payment.

segments.title: Transition to the Gilbreths
segments.summary: The break ends and the hosts introduce Frank and Lillian Gilbreth as the family behind Cheaper by the Dozen.

segments.title: Frank Gilbreth, motion study, and therbligs
segments.summary: Frank Gilbreth's bricklaying efficiency ideas are described, and the couple's firm Gilbreth Inc. broke tasks into eighteen kinds of movements called therbligs. The hosts describe their family life run on efficiency principles and Lillian's view that efficiency buys happiness time, in contrast to Taylor.

segments.title: Taylor's motives and character
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether Taylor was evil, with Josh calling him a misanthrope who stayed indifferent to misuse, and Chuck speculating about undiagnosed conditions.

segments.title: Brandeis, railroad rates, and Taylor's publicity
segments.summary: Louis Brandeis, a progressive lawyer, promoted Taylor's methods before the Interstate Commerce Commission as a way for railroads to avoid rate hikes. The hosts note Taylor's 1911 book The Principles of Scientific Management and how the publicity boosted him.

segments.title: Lillian Gilbreth, home economics, and the kitchen work triangle
segments.summary: After Frank died in 1924, Lillian applied efficiency ideas to the home and is credited with the kitchen work triangle. The hosts mention Flora Rose and Martha Van Rensselaer's domestic science and the Massachusetts superintendent's Greek-instruction cost argument for schools.

segments.title: Kitchen triangle debate and break return
segments.summary: After the break, the hosts briefly revisit whether the kitchen triangle includes the fridge or dishwasher and agree on the fridge.

segments.title: Deskilling, replaceable workers, and the Watertown Arsenal strike
segments.summary: The hosts explain deskilling, where workers do one small task, and its effect on replaceability and wages. They describe the Watertown Arsenal strike of 1911 after a worker refused to be timed, and the federal ban on Taylorism that followed the hearings.

segments.title: Modern echoes: happier workers and algorithmic management
segments.summary: The hosts argue that Taylorism persists, with computers and AI in warehouses and call centers acting as the managers Taylor envisioned, and mention research linking worker happiness to economic outcomes.

segments.title: Consultant anecdote and The Efficiency Expert
segments.summary: Chuck recalls a consultant hired by a former employer to cut staff, and Josh recommends the 1991 film The Efficiency Expert starring Anthony Hopkins. Management consulting is flagged as a possible future episode.

segments.title: Listener mail from Stanley
segments.summary: Stanley writes a thank-you note about listening since 2012 through career and life changes and praises past show moments. The hosts respond and ask for listener mail.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits for Stuff You Should Know as an iHeartRadio production.
